newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba starts testing anti-AIDS vaccine on humans.
newsitem.headline: Cuba starts testing anti-AIDS vaccine on humans.

text.p: Cuba has started testing an anti-AIDS vaccine on humans and 24 young Cuban scientists have been innoculated with the trial Cuban vaccine, Cuban President Fidel Castro said.
Castro made the announcement Saturday night in a speech closing a national science and technology conference.
"We mustn't be too optimistic but we should recognise the effort that our scientists are making," the Cuban leader said, quoted on Sunday by the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina.

He praised what he called the "silent but heroic" action of the 24 Cuban researchers who had volunteered to be innoculated with the Cuban anti-AIDS preparation, which had already been tested on animals.
A combination of widespread AIDS testing and a policy of isolating many AIDS patients in special sanatoriums has helped to slow the spread of the virus in communist-ruled Cuba.
But the Cuban authorities are concerned that the growth of tourism and an increase in sexually transmitted diseases will lead to a faster increase in AIDS cases in the coming years.

Health officials say the number of HIV positive cases registered so far in Cuba rose to 1,408 in November. Of these, 524 had developed the AIDS disease and 373 had died. This compared with 1,196 HIV positive cases reported at the end of 1995 out of Cuba's population of 11 million.
Cuban scientists have already developed and commercialized a vaccine against meningococcal meningitis Type B, which has been used in Latin America and other developing countries.
Cuban researchers are currently testing a vaccine against leptospirosis and are working on an anti-cholera vaccine.
